claims.text: The proposed target alloy is a solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
The target alloy is homogeneous, disordered, and single-phase.
The target alloy lies outside Nb-Ta-based and Ti-rich heavy-transition-metal material classes.
Lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch is the main variable governing the superconducting transition temperature in the target alloy.
Atomic-size mismatch produces enhanced lattice distortion and local strain fields.
Replacing a constituent with an electronically similar element having a significantly larger atomic radius will increase lattice distortion.
The proposed substitution will not substantially change the alloy's average valence-electron count.
Increased lattice distortion modifies the phonon spectrum or phonon density of states.
Increased lattice distortion strengthens the electron-phonon interaction.
The distortion-mediated changes alter the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the phonon spectrum and electron-phonon coupling shift the superconducting transition temperature.
The modified alloy will exhibit a measurable change in Tc relative to the baseline alloy.
The direction and magnitude of the predicted Tc change depend on details of the distortion, phonon spectrum, and electronic density of states.
The baseline alloy has an established superconducting transition temperature under the same processing and measurement conditions.
The hypothesis is restricted to disordered, single-phase HEA solid solutions and excludes multiphase and partially ordered alloys.
Nb-Ta-rich HEA superconductors are the most widely studied HEA-superconductor class.
Prior work also concerns titanium-rich Nb-Ti-based transition-metal systems.
X-ray diffraction can be used in this comparison to assess phase homogeneity, lattice parameters, and strain.
A modified alloy with confirmed enhanced distortion but no statistically significant Tc change relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed governing role of lattice distortion.
